title: Peripheral Skin Cooling During Hypergravity: Effects on Submaximal Cardiopulmonary Performance in the Immediate Post-Exposure Period
content: Background: Aerospace crews may need to perform physical tasks immediately after hy-pergravity (+Gz) exposure. Strategies to preserve submaximal cardiopulmonary perfor-mance in this window remain limited. Objective: To test whether peripheral skin cooling (PSC) applied during +Gz would attenuate residual effects on submaximal cardiopulmo-nary exercise performance. Methods: Eighteen healthy males completed a randomized crossover protocol on a short-arm human centrifuge. Participants underwent a standard-ized +Gz profile (up to +4 Gz) with bilateral thigh cooling or non-cooled control pads. Immediately after +Gz, cycle ergometry was performed to the first ventilatory threshold (VT1) and to volitional exhaustion. Primary outcomes were oxygen uptake (VO₂) and the body-surface-area-indexed VO₂–mean arterial pressure product at VT1. Results: The change from post-+Gz rest in the indexed VO₂–MAP product at VT1 was larger after PSC (+13.2 ± 24.7 L·mmHg·min⁻¹·m⁻², paired t-test p = 0.037). Absolute VO₂ at VT1 was also higher after PSC, but the .the distribution of differences was non-normal; consequently, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test was employed, which yielded no significant difference. No sig-nificant differences were observed at maximal exertion. Linear mixed models showed no significant Condition × Phase interaction for any primary outcome. The VT1 difference was larger when the control session preceded PSC. Conclusions: Bilateral thigh cooling during +Gz was associated with a larger rise in the indexed VO₂–MAP product from rest to VT1. The effect was modest, confined to submaximal intensity, sensitive to session or-der, and not confirmed by the mixed-model interaction or by absolute VO₂ on the preferred non-parametric test. Further studies are required before operational recommendations can be made.
